units: the hall can be entered before the sun comes up
the person in charge lays out equipment on the floor before the group arrives
the participants leave their belongings near the partition
the warm-up pairs a walk with a run
handclaps set the pace of the jumps
a ball-returning drill is done in pairs
the session ends with seated stretching
each student's progress is written down
text: The gym unlocks its doors while the sky is still dark, and the wooden floor gives off a faint damp shine. A short, thickset coach lays out hoops along the center line, then sets a row of low cones beside them. Students file in, drop their bags against the partition, and pull on shoes with pale soles. Warm-up starts with a wide, swinging walk, arms stretched toward the ceiling, and turns into an easy jog around the room. Jumps follow: feet together first, then alternating, while the coach claps out the beat. Next come passes in pairs, each player sending the ball straight back without ever holding it. At the close, everyone sits in a circle and stretches the calves. The coach writes down what each student has managed, then opens the windows to air the room before the next group turns up.

units: the writer finds it contradictory to demand activity while removing open space
school play areas are shrinking in size
empty ground is turned into parking
trips on foot vanish in the name of traffic danger
young children run out of breath on the first flight climbed
the writer blames the surroundings rather than any lack of will
a child with no practice on rough ground absorbs falls badly
the fear of falling deepens the stillness further
the writer asks above all for school surroundings that can be walked
text: We tell children to move more, and then we take away the places where moving is possible. That contradiction wears on me. Schoolyards keep shrinking, empty lots turn into parking, and walking anywhere has been ruled out because the streets count as dangerous. So we get kids who wheeze on the first flight of stairs and tense up the moment an unfamiliar effort is asked of them. Call it what it is: not laziness, but a result. A child who has never run over broken ground cannot absorb a fall. He lands badly, hurts himself, and grows afraid. Fear pins him down harder still, and the loop closes. By all means, add supervised sessions. But make the streets around the schools walkable first. Movement is learned by walking, climbing, and tripping, not only inside a slot penciled onto a timetable.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the head of the swimming group first failed as a competitor
her uneven stroke lost her ground at the turns
she considered leaving the sport
a medical practitioner found a fault in her shoulder position
that fault came from growing too fast
she spent a whole season reworking her technique with video support
her race times came down after the correction
she forbids heavy repetition while the posture is wrong
text: Before she ever ran a group, the swimming coach at the town pool went through a long run of failures. As a teenager she swam length after length without improving, held back at every turn by a jerky, uneven stroke. Her results flattened out, and she came close to leaving the water for good. It took a sports doctor to spot the trouble: a shoulder sitting wrong, the leftover of a growth spurt. Rather than push harder, she gave a whole season to relearning her catch, filmed from below the surface, adjusting where her hand entered the water by fractions. The stroke grew long and steady, and her times fell. Now she puts the same method to work with the swimmers she trains. Film, show, fix one thing per session. She bans endless sets until the position is right, and her group has real staying power.

units: the writer used two different climbing sites in the same season
the first occupies an old and poorly lit building
its holds are smooth from constant use
the routes of the first site call for balance more than pulling
the second site is colorful and its routes change every week
the second encourages bounding and showy movement
the writer prefers the dark site without calling it better
he explains that choice by the attention he must give his feet
text: Two climbing halls took my money in the same season, and nothing about them matches. The first sits under an old market roof and keeps the gloom of a place nobody bothered to repaint. Its holds are worn down, polished by countless palms, and the routes force you to hunt for balance far more than to pull. You climb there slowly, almost without a word, and come down with your forearms burning. The second hall bursts with color. The walls run high, the mats lie thick, and fresh routes go up every week. Everything there invites a leap, a lunge, a movement worth watching. A seasoned climber will find patience in the first and a playground in the second. My preference goes to the dark hall, though I would not call it the better one: it makes me listen to my feet, while the other flatters my arms.

units: the writer sets out on request the method followed since taking the sport up again
he records the length and the speed of every outing
he takes his heart rate on waking while still lying down
he does strength work twice a week without heavy loads
he uses two pairs of shoes according to how long the outing is
he advises drinking before thirst appears
he halts his progression when two sessions in a row feel like a burden
he credits this tracking with the absence of new injuries
text: You asked me to lay out the routine I have followed since starting up again, so here it is, item by item. Load first: every outing goes in the book, total time, average pace, how the last stretch felt. Recovery next: I watch my sleep and take my pulse the moment I wake, still flat on my back. Strength work comes twice a week and no more. Side planks, calf raises, hip extensions, never anything close to a maximum weight. Shoes: two pairs in rotation, a light one for the short outings, a cushioned one for the long ones. Food holds no surprises, apart from one habit, which is drinking before thirst shows up. Mood, last of all: two outings in a row that feel like a chore and I stop pushing. The notebook is an ugly thing, but it holds me upright and has kept me clear of any fresh injury.

units: one question concerns the youngest age for carrying a load
before school age no added weight is needed
the very young child works with his own weight by climbing
the next stage puts the quality of movement above resistance
a light object and a reflection are enough at that stage
the gear has to match the child's build
an adult's equipment must not be taken over
two short training sessions are worth more than one very long one
the exercise stops as soon as the hold of the back gives way
text: A listener writes in to ask how young a child can be and still lift a load safely. The answer runs in stages, and taking them in order is what matters. Before school age, no outside weight serves any purpose whatsoever. The child already has his own body, and he shifts it around well enough by climbing and by rolling. Then comes a stretch of years where learning the movement itself outranks any question of resistance. A light stick and a mirror will do far more good than a loaded bar. A second question concerns the gear, which has to fit the child's own frame and must never simply be borrowed from a grown-up. A third asks about frequency, and a single rule covers it: two short, regular sessions beat one that drags on and on. Watchfulness comes last, and it has to stay sharp. The moment the back starts to round, the exercise ends.

units: a young athlete reports knee pain after three climbs
he had doubled the length of his routes within a week
the coach explains that tendons come along more slowly than breathing capacity
the pain comes from that gap in adaptation
the young man believed himself able to take more
the coach points out that the feeling of ease comes before the tissue grows strong
they agree on a lighter restart and a modest weekly increase
the coach weighs the cost of an ignored injury against that of a short pause
text: A teenager told his coach that his knee began to burn as soon as he reached the third climb of the day. The coach asked him what had changed in his training, and the boy admitted that he had doubled the length of his runs inside a single week. Tendons, the coach said, come along a good deal more slowly than lungs do, and the pain sat right there in the gap between them. The boy answered that he still felt perfectly able to take on more. What feels easy, he was told, arrives well before the tissue is ready for it, and that is exactly what fools beginners. So the two of them settled on a lighter restart, with only a small step up from one week to the next. The boy wanted to know how long that would go on. An injury waved off costs you a season, the coach answered, while caution accepted costs you a handful of outings.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: mail carriers once crossed high ground with no path and no pack animal
one man alone wore himself out before reaching the far end
the letter risked arriving late or being lost
the answer found was to pass the load on
stopping places were set at equal distance
each stop held a rested carrier who left without waiting
the overall speed of the transport was doubled
the carriers stopped holding back since their share was short
this principle of splitting an impossible effort still serves elsewhere
text: Picture messengers who had to cross whole valleys on foot, with no road cut for them and no animal to carry the weight. The work broke bodies, and the flaw in it stated itself plainly enough: one man alone collapses short of the far end, and the letter comes too late or never comes at all. The answer they found was the relay. Shelters went up at an even spacing, each one holding a fresh runner who took the leather pouch and set off again at once. The stretch to be covered in one go turned bearable, and the speed of the whole doubled. Better still, the runners quit saving themselves. Knowing their share was short, they ran it flat out. And there the idea appears that still serves us, from hauling goods to racing in teams: cut an impossible effort into portions a body can hold.

units: what tells the two runners apart is how muscle energy is used
the speed runner has mostly fast-contracting fibers
those fibers are powerful but burn out within moments
the distance runner has fine and slow fibers
those fibers use oxygen without tiring
the speed runner builds a breathing debt that he repays after the effort
the distance runner sets his pace to keep that debt from opening
their training differs between repeated starts and long outings
how the fibers are shared out depends partly on inheritance
text: What sets a sprinter apart from a distance runner, if not the way the muscles spend their energy? The sprinter draws on fast fibers, thick ones, good for a contraction that is short and powerful but dies out almost at once. The distance runner carries slow fibers instead, finer and less quick, which burn oxygen and hardly tire at all. A sprinter produces his force with next to no air, and pays the debt afterward, gasping at the line. The other one holds a pace that never lets that debt open up in the first place. Training shows the split as well. One piles up starts and full recoveries, the other stacks long outings at a steady effort. Work tips the balance one way or the other without ever turning it over, because the share of each fiber type is handed down in part at birth.

units: the narrator recalls a walk along a soaked ridge line
the soles made a sucking noise in the mud
a stone came down the face during the climb
the walk was led by an elderly woman at a steady pace
the other walkers came up scattered
reaching the top happened all at once
a strong wind dried the clothing in a moment
the way down took a gentler side and passed without a word
text: Up on the ridge the mud made every footfall slide out from under us, and that outing has stayed with me above all the others. There was the noise first of all. The suck of soles pulling free, the breath cut short, a single stone rolling off the face into empty air. There was the woman out in front, well past retirement age, climbing without once altering her rhythm, as though the slope had nothing whatever to do with her. There was the group strung out behind her, each of us matching the pace to our own tiredness. And there was the crest, arriving all at once, with a wind that dried our jackets in a handful of seconds. We went down the far side, gentler, telling each other nothing. That silence was worth more than any story, and it comes back whenever a climb looks too steep.
